extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, policymakers, legislators, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Normative recommendations and evaluative standards for restructuring the U.S. patent system to reduce holdup, increase early certainty of rights, and foster an efficient market for patent licenses. Focuses on procedural, remedial, and substantive rule changes (PTO practice, continuation limits, publication, post-grant review, willfulness, remedies, disclosure of license terms, and defenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater early certainty about patent scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent law should provide greater certainty about the nature and scope of patent rights much earlier than at present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieving earlier certainty would require multiple reforms collectively: speeding PTO processing, limiting continuation practice, requiring earlier publication of applications, and instituting mechanisms (peer review, post-grant opposition, gold-plating) to determine validity and scope sooner rather than later. The goal is to let manufacturers and researchers know sooner which rights they must clear so they can make investment decisions without excessive delay or risk of holdup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase PTO resources to process applications faster
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO should be given substantial additional resources so patent applications are processed more quickly and applicants spend less time in uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemley notes application pendency has grown and that reversing this trend is necessary for any system that expects patentees to be cleared pre-investment. This is a prerequisite to reducing delays inherent in a title-search model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict caps on continuation applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Impose strict limits on patentees' ability to delay prosecution through continuation filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting continuations (for example the PTO's proposed three-continuation-as-of-right rule) would reduce uncertainty caused by applicants changing claims long after initial filing and issuance. The paper cites proposals and PTO regulations attempting to cap continuations as a way to prevent indefinite claim-drafting and surprise rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require publication of patent applications earlier and in all cases
rubrics_metrics.description: All patent applications should be published (and preferably earlier than the current eighteen-month standard) so potential users can discover pending rights sooner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandatory publication of applications at or before 18 months (and encouraging earlier publication) would help identify relevant pending patents. The author notes §122(b) and that increasing publication coverage would assist clearing and licensing efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement peer review, post-grant opposition, or similar early-review mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt administrative or community-involvement mechanisms (peer-review, post-grant opposition, gold-plating) to resolve validity and scope earlier than litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include USPTO peer-review pilot projects, post-grant opposition proposals in legislative patent reform, and academic proposals for alternative review procedures. These mechanisms would transfer some resolution of doubtful patents from costly litigation to earlier, potentially cheaper administrative review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an independent invention defense or broaden prior user rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce an independent invention defense or at least robust prior-user rights so manufacturers who independently developed technology need not pay or be punished for inventions they did not copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a matter of equity and practicality (simultaneous invention is common), such defenses would reduce unfair payments for technologies independently developed and lessen incentives to hide innovation. The paper cites several scholarly proposals for independent invention defenses and prior user regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure willful-infringement rules do not discourage reading patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform standards for willful infringement so that companies and researchers are not discouraged from reading patents for fear of creating willfulness exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current doctrines sometimes incentivize counsel or companies to avoid knowledge of others' patents to reduce willfulness risk; Lemley argues rules should be adjusted (building on Seagate and other scholarship) so that clearing and reading patents is not penalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform remedies to reduce holdup (limit injunctions and change reasonable-royalty calculations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Change patent remedy rules to reduce or eliminate holdup by limiting automatic injunctive relief and reforming how reasonable royalties are calculated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eBay v. MercExchange decision is noted as a step toward limiting injunctions; further reform of reasonable royalty calculations is necessary to prevent overcompensation and holdup in component industries. The author advocates reducing the ability of patentees to extract supracompetitive rents during dispute resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require or strongly encourage manufacturers to conduct reasonable patent searches and negotiate in good faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers should be required or at least strongly encouraged to perform a reasonable search for relevant patents and to engage in good-faith licensing negotiations before commercializing technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to conduct reasonable searches and negotiations should trigger potential consequences—enhanced damages, attorneys' fees, or make courts more likely to grant injunctive relief to non-manufacturing patentees. The aim is to inculcate norms of paying for rights used, while accounting for patent invalidity and non-infringing alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require publication of patent license terms
rubrics_metrics.description: To facilitate an efficient market for licenses, patent license terms should be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicizing license terms would make price and licensing information discoverable, enabling better bargaining and market functioning. Lemley and Myhrvold's work on making a patent market is cited in support of this proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate an efficient market for patent licenses via intermediaries and patent-insurance firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage creation of intermediaries (marketplaces, insurers, information providers) that aggregate information, perform searches, provide valuations, and enable arbitrage to smooth license purchases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author imagines patent-insurance firms that would conduct searches and determine necessary licenses (analogous to title insurance) and notes intermediaries are already emerging; legal prerequisites and transparency would accelerate such markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberalize declaratory judgment standards to allow earlier judicial resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Broaden access to declaratory-judgment relief so potential defendants can seek early judicial clarification of patent rights rather than waiting for suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shift from the Federal Circuit's 'reasonable apprehension of imminent suit' standard to the Supreme Court's more liberal MedImmune approach is discussed as facilitating earlier resolution; making declaratory relief more accessible reduces the need to 'ignore' patents until sued.
